title: Teshuvah: the path of return
hookLine: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve; read in full next year
carry: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve, repair
last: NEITHER KNOWS: A GIFT FOR ITS OWN SAKE.

lines: RETURN UNTO THE LORD THY GOD.
A WORD ALL THROUGH JEWISH LIFE.
THE BOOK OF KNOWLEDGE ENDS HERE.
cards: "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God." The prophet Hosea calls it out, and his word, return, runs through Jewish prayer.
Tradition reads Hosea's call on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and names that Shabbat for it. And return is the subject Maimonides chose to close his Book of Knowledge.
Back on day nineteen, you met teshuvah as return, not repentance. Today, the steps of the road.

teach.b: The path of return. Teshuvah: less repentance than turning around, coming back.
Maimonides asks plainly what teshuvah is, and answers with steps. First, recognize and leave. The person stops doing the wrong thing, and takes it out of their thoughts.
You can't turn from a road you won't admit you're on. Second, regret. Not a passing wince, but real sorrow, looking back.
Third, confess. The person puts it into words, out loud. At the very start of these laws, he describes those words: I did this, I am sorry, I am ashamed, I will not do it again.

Fourth, resolve: never to return to that act. And he adds a striking test: the One who knows all hidden things can bear witness that this person won't go back. The resolve has to be real all the way down.
Then one more line, which matters a great deal. For wrongs done to another person, turning to God is not enough. A person must repair what was harmed, and seek the other person's forgiveness.

teach.h: THE PATH RUNS THROUGH THE PEOPLE WE HURT.
teach.b: The path of return runs through the people we hurt. Next year, this path reads these laws in full. Today, just the outline of the road: recognize, regret, confess, resolve.

how: Jews practice teshuvah all year, and especially in the month of Elul and the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur, when it is customary to seek forgiveness from people one has wronged before asking it of God.

games.q: what does “the path of return” mean?
o: a ritual bath taken before the holidays
a pilgrimage walked back home from Jerusalem
turning back from a wrong: regret, confess, resolve

games.q: the path of return — tap the pairs.
p: never to return to the act

s: for Maimonides, feeling sorry inside is the whole of teshuvah
he also requires leaving the act, saying it aloud, and resolving not to return.
the Book of Knowledge ends with the laws of teshuvah
the opening book of the code closes with a way back.
for wrongs against another person, turning to God is enough
Maimonides says the person must repair the harm and seek the other's forgiveness.

games.q: you've hurt a friend. you feel genuinely sorry and you've prayed about it. according to Maimonides, are you done?
o: yes: regret before God is enough.
no: repair the harm and ask your friend's forgiveness.
no: you must wait for next Yom Kippur.
games.why: for wrongs between people, Maimonides says turning to God isn't enough: the person must make it right and seek forgiveness from the one they hurt.

practice: Let one small, true thing come to mind that you'd like to turn from: a sharp tone, a shortcut, a silence where you owed a word. Recognize it, and notice whatever regret is there, without drowning in it.
If it's safe and private, say it once, quietly, in plain words, then picture the next time it comes up, and see yourself turning the other way.

wordCard.voice: The path of return. Teshuvah: in Maimonides' laws, recognizing and leaving a wrong, regretting it, saying it aloud, and resolving not to go back. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, turning back; the name of the laws that close the Book of Knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve, repair. Four steps, one road home, and it runs through the people we hurt. Same time tomorrow.
